briefing_md:
We're in a "hot rates, cold spreads" regime: a global sovereign bond rout is repricing duration while credit and recession models remain unusually sanguine — a divergence that is itself the risk.

The recession dashboard is muted. The ensemble sits at 19.0 (37th percentile of the last 5y), NY Fed probit at 14.3 (10th), EBP probit at 11.4 (16th), and NTFS at 23.7 (19th) — all falling or flat over three months. The near-term forward spread at 0.21pp (77th percentile) and 10y-3m at 0.84pp (82nd) are firmly positive. But that read is built on a curve that is re-steepening for the wrong reason: the 10y at 4.75% is at the 98.5th percentile of five years, up 30bp in three months, while the 2y (+35bp) tells you the front end isn't rallying. With Barr signaling optionality to hike and eurozone HICP at 3.3%, the "no recession" signal is really a "no recession yet, at the cost of a term-premium shock" signal.

Credit conditions look pristine on the surface and that's the anomaly. GZ at 0.86pp is the 3rd percentile of 5y, EBP at -0.30 (16th percentile) is deeply negative, and OFR FSI at -3.03 is essentially a five-year low (3rd percentile). HYG and JNK are flat-to-up on the month despite the duration selloff; LQD is down 2.4% over three months, isolating the pain in IG duration rather than credit risk. The Bloomberg flag on ~$1T of bonds diverging beneath the index, plus the Aston Martin/HPS bondholder fight and Khajuria's "decade-long shakeout" call in private credit, are the tells that dispersion is building under a compressed headline OAS.

Consumer credit is stable but bifurcating. Card 90+ DQ eased to 2.85% and card NCOs to 3.82% (both 42nd percentile), yet single-family mortgage DQ ticked up to 1.86% (74th percentile) — consistent with a housing channel absorbing the 10y move first. The credit impulse at +5.4% of GDP (89th percentile) explains why spreads and the consumer are still cushioned.

Structured finance is leaning in. Record non-QM issuance, PennantPark's CLO reset at SOFR+182, a Brookfield $600mm ABS dividend recap, and 492 royalty and 336 data-center EDGAR filings in 30 days point to esoteric supply absorbing capital. Prime auto senior at 63bp (+4, z=0.37) and card mezz at 80bp (+15, z=0.79) are the first mild wideners worth noting.

watch_items.why: Barr's hike optionality plus Strait of Hormuz tanker strikes make an inflation-driven policy repricing the dominant tail, not recession.

news_digests_recent.summary:
A synchronized global bond rout is the defining market event of the moment. Yields have surged to levels last seen in 2008 across the US, UK, and Europe, with Japan's 10-year bond touching 3.00% for the first time in three decades and the German Bund reaching its highest since 2011. The catalyst is a renewed spike in oil prices tied to escalating Middle East tensions — two supertankers were struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz — which has reignited inflation fears and forced markets to reprice central bank paths higher. The US 30-year Treasury is on its worst extended run since 2006, and US equity futures and stocks have sold off in sympathy.

The Fed's reaction function is unambiguous. Governor Michael Barr signaled readiness to hike further if inflation fails to cool. Evercore's Krishna Guha describes the Fed as "inflation first right now," subordinating jobs data to price and energy dynamics. Fortress's Elizabeth Burton argues rates are structurally poised to go higher, citing unresolved fiscal imbalances. The 10-year yield is widely flagged as breaking out toward 5% and potentially beyond. The ECB faces parallel pressure: eurozone HICP accelerated to 3.3% in August, a near three-year high, cementing expectations for a September hike, with ECB policymaker Olli Rehn warning the Iran conflict could sustain energy inflation.

Credit markets present a stark divergence. Corporate spreads remain unusually compressed even as government yields erupt — Bloomberg flags roughly $1 trillion in bonds telling a different story beneath the surface calm. Achilles Global Management's Sachin Khajuria warns private credit is entering a decade-long shakeout as higher rates expose weaker managers. Apollo is pursuing sports franchise financing at roughly 10% LTV. Aston Martin's financing via BlackRock-owned HPS has triggered a bondholder revolt and legal battle.

In structured finance, activity continues despite the rate backdrop. Non-QM securitization hit a record, signaling a secondary market shift. PennantPark reset a $316.7 million CLO at SOFR plus 182 basis points. Oregon Community Credit Union priced its first auto ABS of 2026, Turning Rock and AerFin closed a second aviation ABS, DLL completed its second securitization of the year, and PennyMac is backing $402.9 million in RMBS with investment-property mortgages. Brookfield is separately pursuing a $600 million dividend recap via an asset-backed transaction on HomeServe.
